caveats.text: Given our safety and security protocols, readers of this manuscript may not execute HELAO-async code with our labo- ratory equipment.

evidence.quote: HELAO-async is being actively developed in two public repositories: [https://github.com/High-Throughput-](https://github.com/High-Throughput-) Experimentation/helao-core encompasses the API data structures and [https://github.com/High-Throughput-](https://github.com/High-Throughput-) Experimentation/helao-async contains instrument drivers, API server congurations, and experiment sequences.
Given our safety and security protocols, readers of this manuscript may not execute HELAO-async code with our labo- ratory equipment.

To create a minimal implementa- tion of Fig. 2, the demo contains two independent Orchestra- tors, each with a dedicated Action Server that simulates the acquisition of electrochemistry data to characterize the over- potential for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). We have packaged previously-acquired electrochemistry data with the demo.

In the demo, the shared Action Server is an active learning agent that manages requests for new acquisition instructions from the two Orchestrators. This shared-resource Action Server runs inde- pendently and is unaffected by the runtime of each Orches- trator
which is demonstrated in the demo by independently starting and stopping the Orchestrators, representing the asynchronous operation of research workows within one or across multiple laboratories.

Running the demo batch script will open ve user interface browsers, two Operators that control the respective Orchestrators, two Visualizers (Observers) that show the data streams from the respective electrochemistry Action Server, and a Visualizer (Observer) for the shared active learning Action Server.
